cards.title: Move SMS outreach from broadcast to iMessage conversations
cards.summary: The 2026 shift in text-based selling: replace automated broadcast SMS with human-sounding iMessage (blue bubble) conversations.
cards.use_when: Deciding which text channel to use for cart recovery, replenishment reminders, winback or VIP outreach, and how to structure those messages.
steps: Accept the source's four foundation premises: (1) send via iMessage/blue bubble rather than green SMS where your audience is iPhone-heavy, (2) meet customers where they already are (Messages is the most-used native iPhone app), (3) sound like a person, not a brand, and (4) design every message to open a dialogue rather than deliver a broadcast.

Audit your existing text flows (abandoned cart, back-in-stock, appointment/webinar reminders, replenishment) for automated-sounding language and rewrite each one so it reads like it came from an individual.
End every outgoing message with a question the customer can answer in a few words, so the thread continues instead of terminating.

Because the source argues SMS deliverability is declining and recipients increasingly reply STOP or mark messages as junk, treat conversational replies — not volume sent — as the channel's success signal.
Verify the current capabilities and compliance posture of any iMessage-sending platform before committing, since tools and carrier rules change.
caveats: The presenter sells an iMessage tool, so treat channel claims as advocacy; A2P/SMS rules still apply to green SMS and consent obligations still exist.
Not all customers use iPhones; the source's 'you must go blue' stance assumes a North American, iPhone-heavy audience.

cards.title: Cut lead-capture friction down to name and phone number
cards.summary: Redesign opt-in forms to collect only a first name and phone number so text outreach can start without friction.
cards.use_when: Designing or trimming the opt-in form for a text list, popup, quiz or landing page that feeds SMS/iMessage flows.
steps: Strip email, company, job title and other qualifying fields from the text opt-in form; keep just name and phone number.
Position the phone number as the single asset you need, because it unlocks a direct personal line of communication with a buyer who is ready now.
Route every downstream automation off that captured number rather than blocking on additional data.
Measure the lift in opt-in rate after reduction, and separately watch the reply rate of the resulting list, since a bigger but unresponsive list is not progress.
Apply the same logic to checkout and post-purchase capture: one field, one purpose, no stacking of marketing questions.
caveats: Removing email can weaken your email list and cross-channel retargeting; if you need email later, collect it inside the conversation rather than on the form.
Consent and disclosure requirements vary by jurisdiction — verify current rules for SMS/iMessage opt-in in your markets.

cards.title: Send first text after a 5-minute delay, in two parts
cards.summary: Wait about five minutes after opt-in, then send an introduction and a low-friction question five seconds later to trigger a reply.
cards.use_when: Setting up the trigger logic and copy for the first message a new text subscriber receives.
steps: Delay the initial outbound text roughly 5 minutes after the opt-in event; the source says this reads as a real person noticing the submission rather than an instant robotic auto-reply.
Message one: introduce yourself by name and company, e.g. 'Hey John, this is Tristan from SendBlue.'
Message two: send about 5 seconds later containing one simple, low-friction, open-ended question — e.g. 'Are you new to X?', 'Have you done X before?', 'How many X projects have you done this year?'
Do not sell or explain anything in the first text; its only job is to earn a reply.
Test the delay window (the source suggests testing 5 versus 7 minutes) and opening word choices against reply rate.
caveats: The 5-minute delay and 'these never-before-discussed secrets' framing are the presenter's heuristics from client work, not benchmarked rules.
Very long delays after high-intent events like cart abandonment may cost the sale — test against the specific flow.

cards.title: Apply the 80-character rule to every text
cards.summary: Keep outgoing texts under about 80 characters (one to two lines) to preserve a natural, human texting tone.
cards.use_when: Writing or auditing copy for automated texts, reminders and follow-ups that customers will read on their phone.
steps: Cap each message at roughly 80 characters — one or two lines maximum.
Avoid walls of text; the source states that long 'brick' messages break the human tone and kill replies.
If the content genuinely needs more room, split it across messages or switch formats (voice note or video) instead of sending a paragraph.
Edit reminders, abandoned-cart nudges and shipping/fulfillment updates to this length so they read like a friend's text rather than a brand notification.
Review a sample of live sent messages and cut anything past the limit as standing QA.
caveats: The 80-character figure is the presenter's working rule of thumb, not a measured optimum; some transactional messages (address changes, order issues) need more detail.

cards.title: Drop opt-out language on iMessage, keep it off green SMS
cards.summary: iMessage conversations can skip 'reply STOP to unsubscribe,' which the source says makes texts feel less corporate and spammy.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to append opt-out and compliance footers to each message in your text flows.
steps: The source argues that because iMessage is not A2P-regulated the way green SMS is, you are free from appending 'reply STOP to unsubscribe' to every message.
Removing the footer restores the personal feel and avoids asking a customer to end the conversation before it starts.
If any part of your program still sends SMS, keep the required opt-out mechanics on those messages and do not copy iMessage-style copy into them.
Consult current carrier, platform and regulatory requirements before dropping any disclosure — rules and enforcement change.
Log and honor opt-out requests through whatever channel they arrive, including conversational replies asking to stop.
caveats: This is the presenter's characterization of iMessage carriage and regulation; verify current legal and platform requirements rather than relying on the claim.
Consumers can still report or block messages, so reply quality — not formatting — ultimately protects deliverability.

cards.title: Hand off to a live human at the first reply
cards.summary: Automation sends the timed first outreach; a real person must take over the moment the customer replies.
cards.use_when: Staffing and routing your text inbox so conversations with high-intent buyers (cart abandoners, VIPs, appointment bookers) are answered by a person.
steps: Treat the first reply as the starting gate, not the finish line — the source says most teams drop the ball by treating it as done.
Build a routing rule that alerts a live agent the instant a reply arrives, and have that human continue the thread.
Give the human the thread history and the goal: keep building trust and move the customer to the next pipeline stage.
Keep automation responsible only for the perfectly timed initial outreach, and humans responsible for connection and closing.
Monitor response latency on replies; slow human takeover undermines the 'this is a person' impression the channel depends on.
caveats: Scaling human handoff requires hiring or reassigning coverage; without it, the strategy collapses back into automation.
After-hours replies need a plan (acknowledge now, respond when staffed) rather than silence.

cards.title: Write texts like a person: small mistakes and abbreviations
cards.summary: Deliberate minor typos and common abbreviations signal a real human on the other end and break corporate tone.
cards.use_when: Drafting conversational copy for follow-ups, appointment confirmations and recovery messages where trust drives the reply.
steps: Insert natural, minimal informality into texts — e.g. 'Just got your call booked for Tuesday. What kind of business do you have?' — the source points to the dropped letters and abbreviated weekday as proof a person wrote it.
Use everyday abbreviations your audience actually uses in their own conversations; avoid slang that would read as forced.
Apply this only to conversational messages, not to transactional copy where clarity matters (order numbers, addresses, prices).
Keep the intent clear — a typo should look like speed, never like carelessness about the customer.
A/B test informal versus polished phrasing and judge by reply rate, since the source's claim that 'only people get replies' is his observation, not a measured law.
caveats: Manufactured mistakes can backfire with B2B or premium audiences who read it as sloppiness; test on your segment.
Do not let informality creep into legal, shipping or price-confirmation text.

cards.title: Use iMessage effects, voice notes and video to revive stalled threads
cards.summary: Channel-specific message formats — text effects, voice notes and short videos — earn attention and rebuild familiarity in text threads.
cards.use_when: Re-engaging customers who have gone quiet (ghosted carts, lapsed subscribers, no-shows) or personalizing high-touch moments like VIP outreach.
steps: Send text effects on key follow-ups to make the message visually stand out; the source names lasers for making a follow-up pop, invisible ink for re-engaging someone who has gone quiet, and confetti for celebrating a win or signup.
Record short voice notes to answer something too long for the 80-character limit, or to remind someone about an upcoming appointment or delivery.
Use short videos to introduce yourself before a call, demo a product, or act as a video sales message.
Match format to intent: voice for reminders and quick answers, video for demos and pre-call introductions, effects for re-engagement.
Test format against text-only on the same reminder or recovery flow — e.g. does a voice note 15 minutes before an appointment beat a plain text reminder?
caveats: Effects and voice/video formats are iMessage features and may not render on other channels or Android recipients.
Production time per message rises sharply; reserve high-effort formats for high-value stages.

cards.title: Track reply rate, show-up rate and close rate instead of opens
cards.summary: Replace delivery and open rates with three engagement metrics that map to money: replies, show-ups and closes.
cards.use_when: Building the reporting dashboard for your text/iMessage programs and deciding what to optimize next.
steps: Drop delivery rate and open rate from your text reporting; the source argues they say little about conversational performance.
Reply rate — the primary metric: are conversations actually starting? Track replies per message sent through each stage of the flow.
Show-up rate — for appointments, demos and webinars: did the people who conversed actually commit and attend?
Close rate — did conversational trust produce purchases, and did it shorten the sales cycle and lift final conversion?
Split-test inputs that plausibly move these numbers: casual greetings versus formal, a 5- versus 7-minute delay, voice versus video reminders, and message length and tone.
Report these three metrics side by side per flow so you can see where a strong reply rate is failing to convert into shows or closes.
caveats: Keep the metrics distinct: reply rate measures conversation initiation, show-up rate measures commitment, close rate measures purchases — do not blend them into one 'conversion' figure.
Reply rate on its own is vanity if replies never progress; pair it with downstream revenue.

cards.title: Split-test iMessage against SMS reply rates before committing budget
cards.summary: The presenter's own tracking reportedly shows about a 2x lift in reply rates from iMessage versus green SMS.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest in an iMessage-sending platform or reallocate spend from SMS for cart recovery, reminders or campaigns.
steps: Set up a clean test where comparable audience segments receive the same content via iMessage and via SMS, and record reply rate for each.
Log results over a meaningful window rather than a single send, since the source's claim is based on roughly two years of client and in-house tracking.
Treat the reported 2x lift as the source's observed result under his conditions, not a guaranteed benchmark — your audience's device mix drives the outcome.
If your list is not iPhone-heavy, measure your actual device composition before assuming the channel advantage applies.
Roll out iMessage where lift is confirmed, keeping SMS for recipients who cannot receive blue-bubble messages.
caveats: The 2x figure comes from the presenter's agency data and is not independently verified.
Channel capability, deliverability and pricing for iMessage tools change frequently — verify the current interface and terms before planning around them.

input.source_name: If I Started SMS Marketing in 2026, I'd Do This.docx
input.text:
14-EML / email and lifecycle

Goes here. SMS marketing strategy, conversational commerce, text-based selling, iMessage outreach, SMS automations (abandoned cart, appointment reminders, opt-in funnels), and SMS metrics (reply rates, show-up rates).

Not here.

Cold calling or outbound B2B sales -> 21-OPS or 19-WLD

Meta Ads or paid media lead generation -> 11-ADC

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details a foundational shift in text-based selling for 2026, advocating for iMessage (blue bubble) outreach over traditional SMS, and outlines specific tactics for maximizing reply rates, maintaining human-to-human trust, and tracking conversational metrics. modules: [EML] topics: [SMS marketing, conversational commerce, list growth] tier: 3 scope_hint: baseline

Topics. SMS marketing / Shifting text-based selling from automated broadcast SMS to human-to-human conversational outreach, specifically emphasizing the transition to iMessage (the "blue bubble") to avoid the spam-associated limitations of traditional green SMS (e.g., mandatory "reply STOP to unsubscribe" language and A2P regulations). Optimizing lead capture funnels by reducing friction to ask only for a name and phone number, and utilizing a 5-minute delay before sending the initial text to simulate natural human behavior. conversational commerce / Driving inbound engagement by utilizing a two-part introductory text template: an introduction followed 5 seconds later by a low-friction, open-ended question designed solely to elicit a reply. Maintaining trust and a conversational tone by adhering to the "80-character rule" (avoiding walls of text), deliberately using common abbreviations or minor typos to appear authentic, and leveraging iMessage-specific features like text effects (e.g., lasers, invisible ink), voice notes, and video messages to build rapport. Mandating a "human handoff" where a live agent takes over the conversation immediately following the first automated reply. list growth / Tracking text-based sales funnels by shifting focus away from delivery and open rates toward engagement-centric metrics: the Reply Rate (the primary indicator of conversation initiation), the Show-Up Rate (for appointments and webinars), and the Close Rate (measuring whether conversational trust shortens the sales cycle and increases final conversions).

Look for. The fundamental shift in modern text-based selling: moving from automated, broadcast SMS to trust-based, conversational iMessage ("blue bubble") outreach. The recommended time delay for the first text message: a 5-minute delay after the lead opts in to simulate human response time. The "80-character rule": keeping text messages under 80 characters (one to two lines maximum) to maintain a natural, non-robotic tone. The "human handoff rule": an automated system handles the initial outreach, but a live human must take over the conversation the moment the lead replies.

Skip. Promotional pitches for the SendBlue iMessage tool, its templates, or links to book a consultation in the video description.

Scope mix. Almost all baseline.

Volume. 1 to 5.

I've spent the last two years sending millions of texts for my clients, analyzing reply rates, and analyzing what actually makes people respond to a text message. And if you're thinking about SMS marketing, SMS outreach, or textbased selling in 2026, there are very important things you need to know to successfully reach your people and drive more sales. In this video, I'm condensing everything that I've learned, all of the breakthroughs, all the best practices, all the templates, all the data into a definitive guide on how to send better text in 2026. It doesn't matter if you're sending your very first text today or if you sent thousands of texts for your business. What I'm going to share is a fundamentally new way to think and go about your texting outreach in 2026 so that you drive more engagement, drive more replies, more trust, and conversions for your business. This video will be separated into five chapters. Chapter one being the foundation of texting in 2026. Chapter two being the art of getting a first reply. Chapter three being beginner level texting secrets. Chapter four being expert level texting secrets. And chapter five being texting metrics and reporting. So feel free to skip ahead to the chapter that interests you the most. Pro tip though, I'd highly recommend starting at chapter 1 because the fundamentals talked about in this section have never been talked about before in the texting industry. Listen up. 2025 marked a significant shift in the texting world where people are tired of getting SMS blasted. We are seeing deliverability of text tanking, people replying stop to text, and even worse, people fully marking your text as junk. All because people are tired of getting sent the exact same texts from all businesses all written with the exact same AI prompts. In 2026, the game is moving entirely towards trustbased human first conversations. If your text sound automated, you are cooked. We have to talk about the four fundamental shifts that will redefine your texting strategy because these secrets have never been discussed yet. This is the true foundation of modern textbased selling, and it starts with accepting four non-negotiable facts about texting in 2026. First, you must go blue. Let's be totally real. People are sick and tired of the green SMS text. They're sick of the text blast, the obvious automations, and the reply stop to unsubscribe line at the end of every single message that they receive. Businesses have somehow found a way to invade and ruin the one channel that people use for personal communications. And people are sick of it. North Americans have iPhones. It's a fact. If people have iPhones and you are texting them a green SMS text, you have to accept that you're not welcome. The only people that are welcome to iPhone users are other iPhone users. People who text blue eye messages and not businesses who text blue eye messages. people who text blue eye messages. This is the foundation of everything that we're going to cover today. So, let me repeat it again. You must start texting your leads, your prospects, and your clients via iMessage in 2026. Second, meet them where they live. You need to know this. Messages is the most used native app on the iPhone. People live in that app. It's where they talk to their friends. It's where they talk to their family. It's where they talk to their partners. And so, your job is to get in there. You need to forget about email. You need to forget about calling, about DMing, and you need to start texting people. Third, be a person and not a business. To get people to reply, you need to embody being a person who texts and not a business who texts. People don't care about a faceless brand sending out texts. They don't care about an automated appointment reminder. They don't care about an automated promotional text. They care about you sending out a text. So be you, be human and people will respond to that. Fourth, conversations not broadcast. In today's age, conversation leads to conversions. Trust leads to conversions. Therefore, we don't want to broadcast and bulk text. We want to build rapport with our leads. Every single text that you send out needs to be designed to open up a dialogue and not just deliver a message. Every message you send has to end with a follow-up question, an opportunity for the lead to bite and to give you one more piece of information about themselves or about their business or about their intentions. Okay, so you've accepted the fundamentals and you're ready to go blue and to be more human in your texting approach. But here's the truth. All that foundation is completely worthless if people don't reply to our texts. Or even worse, if they reply, stop. The entire game of textbased selling in 2026 comes down to one simple urgent metric. We need to get a relevant reply. And if we get that lead to engage with us via text, it's game on. So how exactly do we guarantee that reply? It comes down to these three things. First, reduce all friction.
